CHAPTER 2.6 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.6 · LEARNING AREA 2 · MARCH · APRIL

Investigating graphs

Mirror-image curves, graphs that hug straight lines, tangents on a mountain road: here you put together everything you know about functions. But not as a rigid routine. At the centre there is always a question: where is it steepest? When is it highest? What happens in the long run? You investigate exactly what answers this question.

14 LESSONS4 UNITSPROBLEM, NOT ROUTINE
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • prove symmetry about the $y$-axis and about the origin
  • use asymptotes and the behaviour at the edges of the domain
  • set up tangents and normals, also tangents at points of inflection
  • investigate functions in context with a purpose and interpret the results
  • investigate functions with $\mathrm{e}^x$, $\ln x$ and $\sin x$, also with a parameter, and prove properties
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

A straight line has the gradient 3 and passes through $(1, 1)$. What is its intercept $n$?

$1 = 3 + n \Rightarrow n = -2$

What is the gradient of a line that is perpendicular to a line with gradient 2?

$-\tfrac12$, because $m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1$

What is $(-2)^4$?

16, even powers “swallow” the minus.

$f(x) = x^2$. What is $f'(2)$?

$2 \cdot 2 = 4$

EXPLORATIONSTO GET STARTED · IN GROUPS
MIRROR IMAGES

Use a digital tool to draw $x^2$, $x^3$, $x^4$, $x^5$ and $x^4 - 3x^2 + 1$, $x^3 - 4x$, $x^3 + x^2$.

  • Which graphs are symmetric about the $y$-axis, which about the origin, which not at all?
  • What do the exponents have to do with it?

THE BIKE TOUR

The elevation profile of a tour is $h(x) = -0.2x^3 + 3x^2 + 200$ (height in m, $x$ in km, $0 \le x \le 15$).

  • Where is the highest point? Where is the climb steepest?
  • How steep is that in per cent?
→ Unit 3
THE SKI JUMP

A ski jump ends at the point $P$ of the profile. There the jumper at first flies straight on.

  • In which direction does he take off? Which straight line in mathematics describes this?
  • Which line is perpendicular to the track?
→ Unit 2
UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Symmetry and behaviour at the edges

$f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1$ gives the same value 5 for $x = 2$ and $x = -2$. For $g(x) = x^3 - 4x$, $g(1) = -3$, but $g(-1) = 3$.

In $f$ there are only even powers, the sign of $x$ does not matter: the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. In $g$ there are only odd powers, changing the sign of $x$ changes the sign of the function value: the graph is symmetric about the origin.

KEY POINT · SYMMETRY AND BEHAVIOUR AT THE EDGES

Symmetry about the $y$-axis: $f(-x) = f(x)$ for all $x$. Symmetry about the origin: $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$.

Polynomial functions with only even exponents (including $x^0$) are symmetric about the $y$-axis, with only odd exponents symmetric about the origin.

Behaviour at the edges (chapter 2.1): $x \to \pm\infty$ and approaching points where the function is not defined. Horizontal and vertical asymptotes belong in every sketch.

Saving work: with symmetric graphs you only have to investigate one half. With symmetry about the $y$-axis, a maximum at $x = 2$ means a second one at $x = -2$.

Mixed: $x^3 + x^2$ has even and odd exponents, neither of the two symmetries.

EXAMPLE 1 · PROVING SYMMETRY

Prove: $g(x) = x^3 - 4x$ is symmetric about the origin.

$g(-x) = (-x)^3 - 4(-x) = -x^3 + 4x = -(x^3 - 4x) = -g(x)$. ✓

EXAMPLE 2 · RATIONAL FUNCTION

Investigate $f(x) = \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2 - 4}$ for symmetry and asymptotes.

$f(-x) = f(x)$: symmetric about the $y$-axis. Denominator 0 at $x = \pm 2$, numerator 8 there: vertical asymptotes $x = \pm 2$. Equal degrees: horizontal asymptote $y = 2$.

FIGURE · THE FUNCTION FROM EXAMPLE 2

EXERCISES

Decide without calculating: a) $x^6 - 2x^2$   b) $3x^5 + x$   c) $x^3 + 1$   d) $\cos x$

a) symmetric about the $y$-axis   b) symmetric about the origin   c) no symmetry (the 1 is $x^0$, even)   d) symmetric about the $y$-axis

Prove by calculation that $f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis. Without further calculation, give the second minimum point if one lies at $x \approx 1.22$.

$f(-x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1 = f(x)$. Second minimum point at $x \approx -1.22$ with the same $y$-value.

Show: if $f$ is symmetric about the origin and defined at 0, then $f(0) = 0$.

$f(-0) = -f(0)$, so $f(0) = -f(0)$ and therefore $f(0) = 0$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$f(x) = x^5 - 2x^3$ is …

Only odd exponents.

$f$ is symmetric about the origin, $f(2) = 7$. What is $f(-2)$?

$-7$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Tangents and normals

The tangent to $f(x) = x^2$ at the point $P(1, 1)$ has the gradient $f'(1) = 2$. What is its equation?

We need a line $t(x) = mx + n$ with $m = 2$ through $(1, 1)$: $1 = 2 \cdot 1 + n$, so $n = -1$ and $t(x) = 2x - 1$. The normal is perpendicular to the tangent at $P$. Its gradient is $-\tfrac12$, its equation $n(x) = -\tfrac12 x + \tfrac32$.

KEY POINT · TANGENT AND NORMAL

Tangent at the point $P(x_0, f(x_0))$: $$t(x) = f'(x_0) \cdot (x - x_0) + f(x_0)$$

Normal (for $f'(x_0) \neq 0$): gradient $m_n = -\dfrac{1}{f'(x_0)}$, also through $P$. If $f'(x_0) = 0$, the normal is the vertical line $x = x_0$.

The tangent at a point of inflection is called an inflectional tangent.

Perpendicular: two lines are perpendicular if $m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1$.

Physics: the normal shows the direction of the force with which a smooth track pushes on a body.

INTERACTIVE · TANGENT AND NORMAL

Drag the point of contact. Cyan: tangent, violet dashed: normal. Both axes have the same scale so that “perpendicular” also looks perpendicular.

EXAMPLE 3 · TANGENT AND NORMAL

Find the tangent and the normal to $f(x) = x^3 - 2x$ at the point with $x_0 = 1$.

$f(1) = -1$, $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2$, $f'(1) = 1$. Tangent: $t(x) = 1 \cdot (x - 1) - 1 = x - 2$. Normal: gradient $-1$, $n(x) = -x$.

EXAMPLE 4 · INFLECTIONAL TANGENT

Find the inflectional tangent of $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2$.

$f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 0$ at $x = 1$, point of inflection $(1, 0)$. $f'(1) = 3 - 6 = -3$. $t(x) = -3x + 3$

EXERCISES

Find the tangent to $f(x) = \tfrac12 x^2$ at the point with $x_0 = 2$.

$f(2) = 2$, $f'(2) = 2$: $t(x) = 2(x - 2) + 2 = 2x - 2$

Find the tangent and the normal to $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ at the point $(4, 2)$.

$f'(4) = \tfrac14$: $t(x) = \tfrac14 x + 1$. Normal: gradient $-4$, $n(x) = -4x + 18$.

At which point does the graph of $f(x) = x^2 - 3x$ have a tangent parallel to the line $y = x + 5$?

$f'(x) = 2x - 3 = 1 \Rightarrow x = 2$, point $(2, -2)$.

Find the tangent to $f(x) = \mathrm{e}^x$ at the point $(0, 1)$ and its zero.

$t(x) = x + 1$, zero $x = -1$.

From the point $Q(0, -1)$ tangents are drawn to the standard parabola $f(x) = x^2$. Find the points of contact and the equations of the tangents.

Tangent at the unknown point $(u, u^2)$: $t(x) = 2u(x - u) + u^2$. It must pass through $Q$.

$t(0) = -2u^2 + u^2 = -u^2 = -1 \Rightarrow u = \pm 1$. Points of contact $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, 1)$, tangents $t(x) = 2x - 1$ and $t(x) = -2x - 1$.

TEST YOURSELF!

The tangent to $f(x) = x^2$ at $x_0 = 2$ is $t(x) = 4x + n$. What is $n$?

$4 = 8 + n \Rightarrow n = -4$

The tangent at $P$ has the gradient 4. What is the gradient of the normal?

$-\tfrac14$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Investigating functions in context

The bike tour has the elevation profile $h(x) = -0.2x^3 + 3x^2 + 200$. The question is not “all properties”, but: where is the highest point? Where is the climb steepest?

Highest point: $h'(x) = -0.6x^2 + 6x = -0.6x(x - 10) = 0$ at $x = 0$ and $x = 10$. With the end points $h(0) = 200$, $h(10) = 300$, $h(15) = 200$: the summit is after 10 km at 300 m. Steepest climb: point of inflection where $h''(x) = -1.2x + 6 = 0$, that is after 5 km, with $h'(5) = 15$ m per km, that is a gradient of 1.5%.

KEY POINT · INVESTIGATING WITH A GOAL

1. Translate: which property of the function answers the question? Largest value → extremum (also at the end points). Strongest increase → point of inflection. In the long run → limit.

2. Calculate: only what is needed, with or without digital tools.

3. Interpret and check: answer in context with a unit. Does the result make sense? Does the model hold over the whole range?

Units: the derivative has the unit “$y$-unit per $x$-unit”, here metres per kilometre. 10 m per km is a gradient of 1%.

Domain: in context it is almost always restricted, the end points can be the solution.

FIGURE · ELEVATION PROFILE OF THE BIKE TOUR
EXAMPLE 5 · THE FOUNTAIN

A jet of water has the shape $y = -0.5x^2 + 2x + 1$ (m). How high does it rise? At what angle does it hit the ground at $y = 0$?

$y' = -x + 2 = 0$ at $x = 2$: height $3$ m. Impact: $-0.5x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2 + \sqrt6 \approx 4.45$, $y'(4.45) \approx -2.45$. Angle to the horizontal $\arctan 2.45 \approx 67.8°$.

EXAMPLE 6 · WATER IN A POOL

The rate of inflow into a pool is $r(t) = -t^2 + 6t$ (m³/h, $0 \le t \le 6$). When does most water flow in? What does $r(t) > 0$ mean?

$r'(t) = -2t + 6 = 0$ at $t = 3$: maximum inflow 9 m³/h. As long as $r(t) > 0$, the amount of water increases. How much flows in altogether is answered by integral calculus in Year 13.

EXERCISES

A ball is thrown, its height is $h(t) = -5t^2 + 10t + 1.5$ (m, s). When is it highest, and how high? How fast is it after 0.5 s?

$h'(t) = -10t + 10 = 0$ at $t = 1$, $h(1) = 6.5$ m. $h'(0.5) = 5$ m/s upwards.

The number of visitors to a theme park between 9 a.m. and 7 p.m. is described by $B(t) = -2t^3 + 30t^2$ ($t$ in hours after 9 a.m., $0 \le t \le 10$). When are most people there? When do they stream in fastest?

$B'(t) = -6t^2 + 60t = -6t(t - 10)$: maximum at the end point $t = 10$ (7 p.m.), $B = 1000$. $B''(t) = -12t + 60 = 0$ at $t = 5$: at 2 p.m. with $B'(5) = 150$ people per hour. Criticism: at 7 p.m. hardly the most people are still there. The model rather counts the total number of admissions.

Finish the exploration “The bike tour”: how steep is it at km 2? Where does it go downhill, and how steep is it at the end at km 15?

$h'(2) = 9.6$ m/km (0.96%). Downhill from km 10. $h'(15) = -0.6 \cdot 225 + 90 = -45$ m/km, that is a descent of 4.5%.

A company has the costs $K(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 15x + 10$ (in €1,000, $x$ in 1,000 units). Where do the costs rise most slowly? What does that mean economically?

$K'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 15$, minimum where $K''(x) = 6x - 12 = 0$, so $x = 2$: $K'(2) = 3$. At 2,000 units each additional unit costs least extra (marginal cost minimal). After that production becomes more expensive, for example because of overtime.

TEST YOURSELF!

$h(t) = -5t^2 + 10t + 1.5$. Greatest height in metres?

$h(1) = 6.5$

At which kilometre does the bike tour $h(x) = -0.2x^3 + 3x^2 + 200$ climb most steeply?

$h''(x) = 0$ at $x = 5$

UNIT 42 LESSONS

4Investigating functions with e, ln and sin

With the product and chain rules you can now also differentiate functions such as $(2 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$, $\ln(x^2 + 1)$ or $x + 2\sin x$. The procedure stays the same as for polynomial functions. What is new are the ends: which grows faster, $x^n$ or $\mathrm{e}^x$? And where is $\ln$ defined at all?

KEY POINT · WHAT MATTERS WITH e, ln AND sin

Domain: $\ln(v(x))$ only for $v(x) > 0$.

Ends: $\mathrm{e}^x$ grows faster than any power of $x$. That is why $x^n \mathrm{e}^{-x} \to 0$ for $x \to \infty$, and $\mathrm{e}^x \to 0$ for $x \to -\infty$ produces the horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.

Zeros of $f$, $f'$, $f''$: factor out $\mathrm{e}^{\ldots}$, it is never 0. Sine and cosine give infinitely many solutions: you look for them in a given interval.

With technology: let the CAS give you the higher derivatives of long terms. Deciding what you must investigate and what the results mean is still up to you.

No routine: the curriculum explicitly does not ask for a routine curve sketching, but for the properties asked about and their justification.

FIGURE · THE FUNCTION FROM EXAMPLE 7

Gold: $f(x) = (2 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$ with the maximum point $(1, \mathrm{e})$ and the point of inflection $(0, 2)$. Cyan: the inflectional tangent $y = x + 2$. For $x \to -\infty$ the graph hugs the $x$-axis.

EXAMPLE 7 · A PRODUCT WITH eˣ

Investigate $f(x) = (2 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$: zero, behaviour at the ends, extreme point and point of inflection, inflectional tangent.

Zero at $x = 2$. For $x \to -\infty$, $f(x) \to 0$ (asymptote $y = 0$); for $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to -\infty$.

$f'(x) = (1 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$: maximum point $(1, \mathrm{e})$. $f''(x) = -x\,\mathrm{e}^x$ changes sign at 0: point of inflection $(0, 2)$ with $f'(0) = 1$, inflectional tangent $y = x + 2$.

EXAMPLE 8 · A LOGARITHMIC FUNCTION

Investigate $f(x) = \ln(x^2 + 1)$ for symmetry, extrema and points of inflection.

$x^2 + 1 > 0$, so $D = \mathbb{R}$. $f(-x) = f(x)$: symmetric about the $y$-axis. $f'(x) = \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$: minimum point $(0, 0)$.

With the product and chain rules for $2x \cdot (x^2 + 1)^{-1}$: $f''(x) = \dfrac{2(1 - x^2)}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$. Points of inflection $(\pm 1, \ln 2) \approx (\pm 1, 0.693)$.

EXERCISES

Investigate $f(x) = x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$: zero, behaviour for $x \to \pm\infty$, maximum point, point of inflection.

Zero at 0. For $x \to \infty$: $f(x) \to 0$; for $x \to -\infty$: $f(x) \to -\infty$. $f'(x) = (1 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$: maximum point $\left(1, \tfrac1{\mathrm{e}}\right)$. $f''(x) = (x - 2)\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$: point of inflection $\left(2, \tfrac{2}{\mathrm{e}^2}\right) \approx (2, 0.271)$.

Find the extreme points and points of inflection of $f(x) = x + 2\sin x$ in the interval $(0, 2\pi)$.

$f'(x) = 1 + 2\cos x = 0 \iff \cos x = -\tfrac12$: $x = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $x = \tfrac{4\pi}{3}$. $f''(x) = -2\sin x$: maximum point $\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3} + \sqrt3\right) \approx (2.09, 3.83)$, minimum point $\left(\tfrac{4\pi}{3}, \tfrac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt3\right) \approx (4.19, 2.46)$, point of inflection $(\pi, \pi)$.

Show that $f(x) = x^2 \mathrm{e}^{-x}$ has exactly two points of inflection, and give them. Use $f''(x) = (x^2 - 4x + 2)\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ (CAS or the product rule twice).

$x^2 - 4x + 2 = 0 \iff x = 2 \pm \sqrt2$. Both are simple zeros, $f''$ changes sign there: points of inflection at $x \approx 0.586$ and $x \approx 3.414$.

The sales of a new product are $A(t) = 50t \cdot \mathrm{e}^{-0.1t}$ (items per week, $t$ in weeks). When are most items sold? When do sales fall most sharply?

$A'(t) = 50\,\mathrm{e}^{-0.1t}(1 - 0.1t) = 0$ at $t = 10$: at most $A(10) = 500\,\mathrm{e}^{-1} \approx 184$ items per week. $A''(t) = 0.5\,\mathrm{e}^{-0.1t}(t - 20)$: point of inflection at $t = 20$, where $A'(20) = -50\,\mathrm{e}^{-2} \approx -6.8$. In week 20 sales fall fastest, by about 7 items per week.

For every $k > 0$ let $f_k(x) = x\,\mathrm{e}^{-kx}$. Find the maximum point in terms of $k$ and show: all the maximum points lie on a line through the origin.

$f_k'(x) = (1 - kx)\,\mathrm{e}^{-kx} = 0 \iff x = \tfrac1k$, change of sign from $+$ to $-$: maximum point $\left(\tfrac1k, \tfrac{1}{k\mathrm{e}}\right)$.

With $x = \tfrac1k$, $y = \tfrac{x}{\mathrm{e}}$: all the maximum points lie on $y = \tfrac1{\mathrm{e}}\,x$.

TEST YOURSELF!

At which point does $f(x) = x\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ have its point of inflection?

$f''(x) = (x - 2)\,\mathrm{e}^{-x}$

What is the $y$-value of the maximum point of $f(x) = (2 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$ (three decimal places)?

$f(1) = \mathrm{e} \approx 2.718$

$f(x) = \ln(x^2 + 1)$. What is $f'(1)$?

$\tfrac{2 \cdot 1}{1 + 1} = 1$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Investigate $f(x) = x^3 - 4x$ for symmetry, zeros, turning points and points of inflection and sketch the graph.

Symmetric about the origin. Zeros $0$, $\pm 2$. $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} \approx \pm 1.15$: maximum $(-1.15, 3.08)$, minimum $(1.15, -3.08)$. Point of inflection $(0, 0)$.

Find the inflectional tangent of $f(x) = x^3 - 4x$. At what angle does the graph cut the $x$-axis at the origin?

$t(x) = -4x$. Angle: $\arctan 4 \approx 76°$ to the $x$-axis (measured downwards).

Connecting with chapter 2.1: sketch $f(x) = \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2 - 4}$ with all asymptotes. Where does the graph have a turning point?

From the symmetry and the shape: maximum $(0, 0)$ between the poles (the values there are $\le 0$). You confirm this by calculation in Year 13 with the quotient rule.

Show: the tangents to $f(x) = x^2$ at the points $(a, a^2)$ and $\left(-\tfrac{1}{4a}, \tfrac{1}{16a^2}\right)$ are perpendicular to each other.

Gradients $2a$ and $2 \cdot \left(-\tfrac{1}{4a}\right) = -\tfrac{1}{2a}$. Product $-1$. ✓

EXCURSIONA WORD FROM ANTIQUITY

Where the asymptote comes from

Around 200 BC Apollonius of Perga wrote eight books on conic sections, the curves that appear when you cut a cone with a plane: circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola. The names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola come from him.

In the second book he investigates two lines which the branches of a hyperbola approach more and more without ever reaching them. He called them asymptotos, “not falling together”. The graph of $\tfrac1x$ is such a hyperbola, its asymptotes are the two coordinate axes.

Source: Apollonius of Perga: Conics, book II.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

SYMMETRY

$f(-x) = f(x)$: about the $y$-axis · $f(-x) = -f(x)$: about the origin.

$x^4 - 3x^2 + 1$ · $x^3 - 4x$

TANGENT

$t(x) = f'(x_0)(x - x_0) + f(x_0)$

$x^2$ at 1: $t(x) = 2x - 1$

NORMAL

Gradient $-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_0)}$, through the same point.

$x^2$ at 1: $n(x) = -\tfrac12 x + \tfrac32$

e, ln AND sin

Check the domain, factor out $\mathrm{e}^{\ldots}$, $\mathrm{e}^x$ beats every power.

$(2 - x)\,\mathrm{e}^x$: maximum point $(1, \mathrm{e})$, inflectional tangent $y = x + 2$

IN CONTEXT

Translate the question, calculate with a purpose, interpret with a unit, check the model.

Bike tour: summit at km 10, steepest climb at km 5
